Explore the presentation

Quality extends beyond the prompt

A capable model is one component of a production agent. The surrounding system must handle tool failures, isolate state, constrain actions, preserve evidence and detect regressions.

This executive deck connects those responsibilities to a data-product approach: manage inputs, memory and outputs with explicit contracts, quality measures and lineage. It maps that approach to Dataknobs Kreate, Kontrols and Knobs.

Presentation context: Explanations summarize the supplied Dataknobs deck. Platform capabilities, alignment claims and delivery estimates are source-deck claims, not independent certification or benchmark results.

01 · From prompt quality to run quality

SLIDE 01 / 12

Agent engineering: from prompts to production

This executive presentation frames reliable agents as a systems and data-product challenge. It connects orchestration, tools, memory, observability and governance to the quality of complete runs.

Back to slide index ↑
SLIDE 02 / 12

Why agents fail after the demo

The deck identifies silent tool errors, repeated actions, unreproducible failures, memory isolation problems, prompt injection and model regressions. Improving a prompt may help behavior, but these failure modes also require controls around execution and state.

Back to slide index ↑
SLIDE 03 / 12

The unit of quality becomes the run

Prompt engineering focuses on individual interactions; agent engineering also manages tool contracts, handoffs, recovery and action permissions. A complete run must be observable and evaluable across its steps, not just judged by its final wording.

Back to slide index ↑

02 · Architecture, data products and risk

SLIDE 04 / 12

The six-layer production stack

The proposed stack covers interaction, orchestration, tools, state and memory, observability, and safety/governance. The governance plane spans the other layers through policy checks, approvals and an audit trail.

Back to slide index ↑
SLIDE 05 / 12

Agent artifacts as data products

Inputs, tool responses, memory records and final outputs are treated as managed data artifacts. The deck emphasizes schema versions, ownership, retention expectations and lineage tied to a run identifier.

Back to slide index ↑
SLIDE 06 / 12

Production risks and failure controls

The risk map covers unauthorized actions or data exposure, silent regressions, excessive cost and latency, and failures that cannot be reproduced. The slide’s severity labels and cost multipliers are illustrative; teams should assess impact using their own workloads and incident criteria.

Back to slide index ↑

03 · Platform approach and measurement

SLIDE 07 / 12

The Dataknobs approach

The presentation positions Kreate around building data products, Kontrols around governance and validation, and Knobs around optimization and human involvement. These are the platform roles described by the source deck.

Back to slide index ↑
SLIDE 08 / 12

Mapping capabilities to engineering gaps

The deck maps brittle tools, memory leakage, output errors and missing audit trails to contracts, governance, validation and lineage. Its standards-alignment statements are product positioning, not independent evidence of certification or legal compliance.

Back to slide index ↑
SLIDE 09 / 12

Four categories of production metrics

Outcome metrics cover task success, acceptance and resolution time. Tool and data metrics cover call accuracy, errors, schema conformance, completeness and grounding. Safety metrics cover attack success, guardrail triggers and sensitive-data leakage; each needs a defined test population and measurement method.

Back to slide index ↑

04 · Roadmap and next steps

SLIDE 10 / 12

A staged migration to production

The proposed ten-week plan moves from specifications, permissions and tracing to an evaluated MVP, hardening, and monitored rollout. This is a planning sequence rather than a delivery guarantee; readiness depends on passing the relevant evaluation and operational gates.

Back to slide index ↑
SLIDE 11 / 12

Build versus platform

The source compares custom implementation with shared platform capabilities for schemas, memory, lineage, guardrails and release gates. Its time-to-production figures are promotional estimates rather than an independently measured benchmark. A build decision should compare requirements, integration effort and demonstrated controls.

Back to slide index ↑
SLIDE 12 / 12

From reliable runs to governed outputs

The closing message links prompt quality, dependable execution and managed data outputs. The deck invites a Dataknobs demo to discuss how the proposed platform approach fits an enterprise workflow.

Questions answered

What is agent engineering?

Designing and operating the complete agent system: orchestration, tools, state, evaluation, observability and action controls.

How does it differ from prompt engineering?

Prompt engineering improves model interactions. Agent engineering also addresses complete runs, handoffs, recovery, permissions and operational behavior.

What are the six layers?

Interaction, orchestration, tools, state and memory, observability, and safety/governance.

Why treat outputs as data products?

Outputs and intermediate artifacts need ownership, schemas, quality checks, retention policies and traceable lineage.

Which metrics matter?

The deck groups metrics into outcomes, tool quality, data-product quality and security/safety.

Is the ten-week roadmap a guarantee?

No. It is an illustrative migration plan. Readiness depends on scope, integrations, evaluation and operational requirements.
